newsitem.title: USA: Bidders pay millions for Princess Diana's gowns.
newsitem.headline: Bidders pay millions for Princess Diana's gowns.

text.p: Princess Diana's glamorous cast-off gowns sold for more than $3.2 million on Wednesday in what auctioneers said was a record price for a charity auction, not to mention second-hand clothes.

The 79 dresses that the princess wore to such far-flung places as Japan, Pakistan, South Korea and the Reagan White House during her 15-year-marriage to Britain's Prince Charles were eagerly snapped up as a crowd of 1,100 people at Christie's clapped, cheered, and whistled.

But the 35-year-old princess, whose fairy-tale marriage ended in bitter separation and divorce, slept through it all, oblivious to the spirited bidding by people ranging from women who wished they were her to companies and museums seeking an association with her name and fame.
At home in London while the sale went on, the Princess had left instructions with Christie's chairman Lord Hindlip not to call and wake her with the results. "I'll call in the morning," Hindlip said.

A blue silk velvet dress Princess Diana wore for a state dinner hosted by President Ronald Reagan at the White House, in which she danced with film star John Travolta, sold for $222,500, a record auction price for a costume.
Ironically it surpassed the previous record of $145,000 paid for the costume Travolta wore in the hit film "Saturday Night Fever".
Hindlip said the buyer of the dress was an anonymous American male collector whom he descrined as "a great fan of the princess."
The second highest price of the evening was $151,000 for a white strapless evening dress and cropped jacket that the princess wore on a state visit to Hong Kong and to film premieres.
Fashion commentators called it her "Elvis" dress because of its uplifted collar on the white jacket.

The outfit was bought by the Franklin Mint which specialises in selling plates, commemorative coins, dolls and mostly recently a replica of a three-strand necklace of fake pearls once owned by Jacqueline Kennedy Onassis.
"We plan to put in on display at our museum of 20th century icons right next to the original of Jackie O's fake pearls," said the Mint's spokeswoman Mona Astra Liss.
Liss said the mint had no plans to produce replicas of the dress.
Many of the bidders in the audience at Christie's were women who admired the princess but admitted they were not sure what they would do with the dresses once they bought them.

"I've been following her for a long, long time and I've bought a bit of history but I don't know what I am going to do with it," said Donna Coffin from the Chicago suburb of Lake Forest who paid $32,000 for a dress. "I may have to go to the gym," she added.

Washington Post columnist Anne Gioer had warned the readers of her "Reliable Source" column that the sale was "a pig in the poke" because Christie's won't let you try the dresses on or bring them back if they don't fit.
Proceeds from the sale of the outfits will go to the princess's favourite charities, including breast cancer research and the fight against AIDS.
Only a handful of the buyers were British, but they included a British newspaper which bought a $40,000 number and plans to give it away in a competition.
Hindlip said 83 percent of the buyers were American, 11 percent from Europe, 4 percent from Asia and the rest from South America and Australia.
The most controversial dress of the evening was bought by a Scottish collector.

It was the black silk crepe dress Diana wore to a dinner in 1993 the night her ex-husband Prince Charles went on British television and admitted he had had an affair with Camilla Parker Bowles. It sold for $74,000.
The British press had labelled that frock, Diana's "Up Yours" dress.
